title: Soon ashes
hookLine: soon you'll be ashes; meanwhile, revere and do good (Meditations 5.33)

lines: WE KEEP THE WORD AT A DISTANCE.
cards: Ashes is a word people tend to keep at a distance, for funerals and a few solemn days a year. Marcus Aurelius kept it closer. In book five, entry thirty-three, he writes it to himself very plainly: you'll be ashes soon.
Then, in the same breath, he asks what a person should do with the time in between. His answer is short, and it isn't gloomy at all. It's a to-do list.

teach.h: SOON ASHES, AND A NAME, OR NOT EVEN.
teach.b: Soon, very soon, Marcus writes, you'll be ashes, or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name. And a name is only a sound and an echo. Then he looks at what people spend their lives fighting over.
The things most prized in life, he says, are empty and small: puppies snapping at each other, children quarreling, laughing, and then crying a minute later.

He borrows a phrase from the Greek poet Hesiod, about virtues fleeing the wide earth for Olympus, and applies it to faithfulness, modesty, justice and truth. A wry picture of a world that often forgets what matters.
So what holds him here, he asks, since the things we sense are always changing and our senses are easily fooled? His answer: wait calmly for the end, whatever it turns out to be.
And meanwhile, what's enough? To revere the gods and speak well of them.
To do good to people. To bear with them, and to hold back. And to remember that whatever lies outside your own small flesh and breath is not yours and not up to you.
Marcus doesn't use ashes to stop himself living. He uses it to clear the desk. The squabbles drop off.
What's left fits on a card: reverence, kindness, patience, restraint. For him, reverence meant the gods of Stoic belief; readers on many paths keep that part in their own words, or in none.
The rest is open to anyone: do good, now, while there's a now.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes use the plain reminder of Meditations 5.33, 'soon ashes', to clear away small quarrels and do one good act right away.

o: an old Roman funeral rite for honoring the dead
a reminder of death that clears room to do good now
a gloomy saying meant to make life feel pointless

games.q: you're still fuming over a petty family dispute about who said what at dinner. what fits Meditations 5.33?
o: keep the argument going until you win.
let it drop, and do one good thing meanwhile.
games.why: Marcus calls such quarrels puppies snapping and children crying; meanwhile, what's enough is to do good and bear with people.

practice: Say the word quietly to yourself, ashes, and let it be plain, not frightening. Then feel your breath, warm and still here.
Meanwhile: bring to mind one small good act within reach, a message, a kindness, a bit of patience, and let that be enough.

wordCard.voice: Soon ashes. Marcus reminds himself he'll soon be ashes and a name; meanwhile, it's enough to revere, to do good, and to bear with people. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'ashes': the plain word Marcus uses for what he will soon be.

carryVoice: Your line: meanwhile, do good. Reverence, kindness, patience, restraint. Day five hundred seventy-one, done.
